title: Experienced Game Devs: What are the subtle tells of a novice dev.
author: MosesSecondofHisName
selftext:
I think it's very clear when a game was made by an experienced dev vs when it was made by an amateur, but as an amateur myself, I can't really articulate why unless it's something and obvious.

So for the experienced devs, what are the things that are obvious to you (but subtle to amateurs) that let you look at a game and tell within a few seconds that the dev is a novice?

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
There's a few of em I see that show up consistently. It's not just AI games though, this happened in indie spaces all the time too before AI.
 - Lack of polish. They usually start posting like they're nearly done with the game as soon as they have something visible but it's clearly just a tech demo or an early prototype. There's obvious bugs, visual polish is lacking, the design seems incoherent, etc.
 - Genre/game mashup based design. Their game usually is X and Y with a little bit of Z smashed together without the game having own identity. Stuff like "I made GTA but in space with lasers!". That's not to say you can't borrow ideas from other games, but a mashup vs an inspired design is usually pretty obvious. Each piece of the game should have a reason for being there and the game needs it's own identity even if it's very similar to an existing game.
 - The videos they show don't really showcase the game in the best light and the context is usually "look what AI did!" instead of "look at my awesome game!". Like I get it, your excited and it is cool. But most other people won't care about your game more than you do, you have to hook them on the game alone not your vision of what it should be.
 - A collection of features with no design at all. This one is adjacent to the mashup failure, but the game looks like a lot of features piled in without any real written reason for them to exist in the game at all. Sometimes that's fine for more arcade style games but generally nothing should feel like it was bolted on.
 - A lack of progression and a game loop. The game itself might be fun as a tech demo but there's no reason to keep playing it beyond a round or two. There's nothing to unlock, there's nothing to discover, it's just a fun set of mechanics with no binding.

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: This is a reasonable take about game dev as a whole.  Im crossing the line from hobby into trying to make a commercial product, and its tough to fight the temptation to show off things too early.

replies.author: TechgeekOne
replies.body:
It happens even inside studios too. I had to learn to fight the temptation to show off a feature to other teams too early because very often they can't see beyond what is right in front of them. And if it's not visible, it doesn't exist in their minds. 

I remember showing off some fancy internal ECS thing I did in Unreal for a feature they wanted but because I didn't have anything visibly flashy ready at the time the reception by design was terrible. When I finally got it hooked up to pretty graphics and working for the real in-game mechanic, then they suddenly they understood the vision lol.

replies.author: adelie42
replies.body:
As an aspiring hobbyist since the Apple II came out trying to move towards legit part time solo indie developer, I strongly agree and you make me feel really good about details I have put an obnoxious number of hours into addressing. The most concrete thing I can point to is that I get distracted from improving the game because I just want to play it endlessly, and every play I take pages of notes. Getting in to all the polish was initially intimidating and I feared it would be endless ruminating about perfectionism, but it is actually getting honed into a coherent, clean, style.

The one thing I will really take away form your share (which I greatly appreciate) that I keep avoiding, is a story arc that fully connects the beginning to the end and explaining how each step plays a role. I waited a very long time to even put in a minimalist title screen because I wanted instant action at launch. The compromise is three buttons over a essentially paused game ready to play on launch. The world and the game are the tutorial (I loved and was inspired by that recent article about how the original Super Mario Brothers mastered this). If it isn't self-explanatory on use, a tutorial page explaining why you couldn't be bothered to make a better design isn't going to save it. And to story, Nintendo built an empire on "your princess is in a different castle", not 5 minute cut scenes and dialog every two minutes.

>Their game usually is X and Y with a little bit of Z smashed together without the game having own identity.

Yeah, like you picked matte paper, watercolor and acrylic, with a little ink and you think you are going to impress someone with a receipt from the craft store.

replies.author: MosesSecondofHisName
replies.body: The genre mashup thing is so good. It's tough because so many professionally designed games are marketed as X meets Y style mashups, so I think it's easy to assume that's how to build a game. But I imagine that's often a marketing thing tacked on after the fact to communicate the game to its audience, not something that guides design when building.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: novice seems so impressed they did anything, and forget to include actual game systems that players want to play and work togethere, its  more then just moving pixels on a screen

replies.author: count023
replies.body:
An experience dev also doesn't just add things because they look cool, or in the case of say a fan game, because it's "canon". A lot of licensed titles for franchises for instance are  a good example of the thinking of a pro game dev. An experienced one focuses on gameplay and enjoyability over accuracy, because 100% accurate to the source material does not necessarily equate to an enjoyable time.

And in original content of course, same general principle. An experienced dev knows what gameplay elements do not feel fun or would not be enjoyable (unless you work fro Ubisoft), and tend to steer away from "cool" because tends to be a lot of work for a little pay off that the players generally wont appreciate anyway.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
I have been reviewing games from this sub and usually it is the vibe and the lack of consideration in some obvious areas. 

for example, both an experienced dev and a novice dev can be making a game with the default claude vibe coded UI but the novice devs would have buttons all in a row or arrange the buttons in some weird order. 

novice devs also dont care enough about "onboarding" i.e. making the tutorial/how-to-play intuitive and easy to follow. 

and experienced devs usually approach it with a plan e.g. the landing page has a mini-ad that says "hey btw, we got an app version if you want to play on phones" or things like "join our discord" 

novice devs usually just stop at "I have a game" and there isn't a bigger plan to market/promote the game. 

I am still learning how to up my "game" but I am starting to see some patterns

replies.author: adelie42
replies.body: Thoughts on "tutorial", I have seen some critics of "tutorials" where essentially you are explaining how the game plays because it doesn't actually make sense on its own. While I hate the term "intuitive", I think great games teach you how to play by just playing it. Allow things to reveal themselves through progression. And I agree that can be really hard, I just think the best games have no separate "here's a tutorial you need to play before actually playing". They just make it fun to play.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
that's one way to solve the problem but I haven't seen that often in indie games. 

the standard mobile/browser game style tutorials help a lot imo: make a skippable tutorial with highlights and indicators 

I have also seen games where it is weirdly made even with the tutorial

games with experienced devs tend to have a smoother experience overall (I suspect that some of them works at game studios so they bring their usual conventions to their own personal projects)

comments.author: GoblinMatr0n
comments.body:
I don't consider myself a experienced game dev, but my real job is being a dev. I've been following extracredit game dev video on youtube for many years now. Thing is I never learned a language that work on a game engine but always day-dreamed to make my own game. 

With AI now, i fully get to do so, but what i think a lot of peep in this sub right now skip is that when vibe coding a game, its very important, you aren't a dev. You're more like CEO/CTO. 

So this what I see the most in this sub, people rush the game they wanna make. if you go to fast and add to many feature too soon, its a whole of spaghetti and the ai design slapped on top. for sure no one really wanna play that. 

When making a game you gotta elaborate first on what would conclude the MVP of your game. Have friend or ask here for people feedback on your mechanic and the overall gameplay. Then you need a good plan for the alpha development and then beta. Even if you're making your game with AI, unless its a very small game with barely any gameplay in it, it should take you months to calibrate the thing and making it good. Have a trello board or jira or anything for planning it. You need a plan and a vision like a real CEO/CTO.

comments.author: Top_Biscotti_7196
comments.body: Getting excited and posting too early.

comments.author: A_Sword_Saint
comments.body:
Lots of things. No clear core loop that all the mechanics on display have a role in. A lack of understanding and communicating a clear vision of where the games design space sits in the market and how it differentiates, not knowing who your audience is or what excites them, bloated lists of features that don't arent cohesive. Controls and ui that are neither custom tailored to work well for your game or referenced directly from the market so that they are intuitive and smooth to use. A clear lack of playtesting showing through in the balance and user experience. Shallow, if any, alignment between art direction and gameplay. 

You could go on and on.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
I will start with that I am engineer first and I picking up design tasks for fun and fixing up our designers design after we have goal for a feature, so take my opinion with grain of salt.

I think the problem is that there is not a single good answer for this question. I think, most people thinking about design and UX as some general knowledge, what everyone can do just like that. I do not think that is true.

I think it boils down into these things:

Knowledge, there are tons of books research papers about players game design and UX, like there is insane amount of research about how they think what’s are the archetypes etc. Picking target audience is the first step, second step is understanding them.

Empathy and self reflection. You basically try to look at your self from outside and understand how the game makes you feel, or what you missing. Understanding the players through player test is extremely valuable too.

Intuition is the last one, after a time, it just happens you feel it, your brain connects invisible dots and oh that’s how!

Last but not least you need to accept there are no dumb players, just bad UX and design. Some games fail big time, because they blame the players and never the player is to blame.

Last thing what I would like to share is a small example of ux failure in a great game and how many considerations a UX designer would need to take into account to mitigate it.

In xcom if you want to leave a mission without finishing it your soldiers need to be in extraction zone, or you lose them. My ex(by the way UX designer) , wanted to abandon the mission and she clicked on the red pop up on “abandon the mission”, it happened so fast I couldn’t even warn her. Obviously she wasn’t happy she lost the soldiers.

Now this pop up fails in so many ways:  
You get a red popup, you connect the red thing to important and dangerous things, however when that popup opens up the player knows they will fail the mission, means they will connect the red to it.

Now some things to consider:  
The players will mostly leave the missions, from extraction zone, because the mission requires it.  
That means players in 99% cases will not want to abandon a mission, this means they will not learn this behaviour. Even if the players want to abandon a mission there is high chance they do not want to left soldiers behind.

So based on this information:  
You can make a less shine red popup and highlight the part of the text which is about losing soldiers with bright red.  
And because players, will not see this window many times you can just make them wait 5 seconds or even more, they will get bored and they will read the text.

In this case you probably 100% mitigate the problem.

I want to mention most of design decisions are really this complex in nature and that is why it is actually hard to create great game.

I would suggest read books about player ux/design, it will open your eyes how complex is that problem.

It is not simpler at all then engineering, just people think it can be done by gut feeling, it cannot be if you do not build your intuition by knowledge and experience.

replies.author: Strategic_Sage
replies.body:
I clearly don't have nearly your knowledge in general here, but I should say I can be confident that some of what you are saying does not reflect the reality I see.  Players react wildly different to the same UI.  Dumb players absolutely do exist, but a common thing I see is the following:

Players of game x complain about UI.  They say why can't it be more like game y, as an example of how it 'should be done' 

Ok, go to game y community.  What do you find?  Segment of the community that says the UI is terrible, wishing it was like game x or game z.  And around and around the circle you go.  

It seems very evident that there's no such thing as a UI that just works for anything approaching all players.  It's one of those aspects where a huge amount of player preference and variance is at play.  There always and forever will be a significant amount of players who don't like it, no matter what you do with it.  There certainly are better and worse ui approaches of course, but there's a pretty low ceiling on the degree to which it can be considered objectively good

comments.author: Cold-Jackfruit1076
comments.body:
For me, one of the biggest tells is when two or more systems work well together *in principle*, but don't mesh in practice -- that is, they built those systems without a clear use case and now they can't take them out without dismantling most of the project:

* You can’t balance the economy because the dual-wielding system breaks the damage scaling.
* You can’t fix the AI because the AI pathfinding is tied to the dual-wielding combat logic.
* You can’t improve the UI because the UI is hardcoded to display stats for features that don’t actually do anything useful.

In the end, dual-wielding ends up tacked onto a combat system that doesn't *need* it.
